facts.text: Friendship Heights Village was officially created on March 20, 1914 as a special taxing district, giving residents limited local control while staying under Montgomery County.
The 1914 law allowed a 10‑cent per $100 tax to fund street work and sanitation, marking Friendship Heights' shift from farmland to suburb.
Humphrey Friendship Park opened in 1970, and the Village Center followed in 1986, giving residents green space and a hub for gatherings.
Friendship Heights sits beside the Red Line Metro station, and local groups now run the Page Park Project to protect nearby green space.
The 1966 opening of the Friendship Heights Metrorail station sparked a boom, leading to towers like The Irene and The Willoughby that dominate the skyline.
Friendship Heights Village covers just 34 acres, yet its high‑rise buildings make its density rival that of Manhattan.
